claims.text: Applying high external hydrostatic pressure during rapid melt quenching improves glass-forming ability relative to ambient-pressure quenching.
Applying high external hydrostatic pressure during rapid melt quenching enhances the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy investigated in the liquid-to-solid quenching context.
The proposed pressure range for pressure-assisted quenching is 1–3 GPa.
A cooling rate of approximately 10^5 K/s can be produced by melt-spinning this alloy.
Uniform pressure application is required for the proposed beneficial effect.
Pressure-assisted quenching enhances short-range atomic ordering in the rapidly solidified alloy.
Pressure-assisted quenching suppresses the free-volume distribution in the rapidly solidified alloy.
External pressure reduces atomic mobility and diffusion during solidification.
Pressure-induced reduction of mobility and diffusion retards crystal nucleation kinetics.
Pressure-induced reduction of mobility and diffusion retards crystal growth.
External pressure deepens the undercooling attained during quenching.
Retarded crystallization and deeper undercooling produce a more robust and thermally stable amorphous structure.
High-pressure-quenched samples will be fully amorphous.
High-pressure-quenched samples will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than ambient-pressure samples.
High-pressure quenching will broaden the critical-cooling-rate margin relative to ambient-pressure quenching.
Non-uniform pressure distribution may limit the proposed effect.
Pressures above 3 GPa may induce unwanted microstructural effects.
Cooling rates below approximately 10^5 K/s may be insufficient for amorphization of this alloy.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature and a more homogeneous amorphous structure would falsify the hypothesis.
